10-11

  • N: [ ... ] ... šabiṣ | ibrī | inakkud | pagrum
  • T: ‘[…] is gripped, my friend, the body palpitates.
  • L: šabiṣ ← šapāṣu I “~ to clasp, enfold”; ibrī ← ibru I “friend, colleague”; inakkud ← nakādu I “to beat, throb Bab., MA”; pagrum ← pagru I “pl. pagrū, jB also f., NB also pagrānu body”
  • Note: See [RN117: 206–207]: “In his transliteration of the opening lines of the tablet in Essays Pope ([RN163: 31], Foster reads the end of the line as úr-ba-ri but without translating. There seem to be too many wedges present to read {gišEREN} (so [RN580: 80, fn. 1]) and I have kept to the original reading of Jastrow and Clay. Tournay and Shaffer read [im-ta]-aq-qu₂-ut ([RN580: 80, fn. 2]). The trace at the beginning of the line precludes this, but i#-[m]a-aq-qu₂-ut is possible. They also sustain the old reading of the following word as wa-aq-rum but to my eyes the antepenultimate sign is pa, not wa. As I understand it, Enkidu is describing his intense physical reaction to whatever terrifying and impossible undertaking (see l. 17) Gilgameš has proposed in the lacuna.”
BabaOB1 i 10-11. [x (x) x]-x-im?# ša#-bi-iṣ ib?#-ri# | i#-[n]a?-ak#-ku-ud pa-ag-rum

12-13

  • N: a[m-mīni]m | tahših || a[nn]iam | ep[ē]šam
  • T: Why do you desire to do this thing?
  • L: a[m-mīni]m ← ammīni I “why?”; tahših ← hašāhu I “to need, desire”; a[nn]iam ← annû I “OB occas. with nunation this, those”; ep[ē]šam ← epēšu I “action, behaviour OB e. damqum good behaviour”
  • Parallels: L I.4 OB "III" 113-114
BabaOB1 i 12-13. a[m-mi-ni]m ta-ah-ši-ih | a[n-n]i-a-am e#-p[e]-ša-am

14-15

  • N: [ ... ] ... mimma [ ... ] ... | mādiš | [t]ahših
  • T: […] anything […] do you desire so much?
  • L: mimma ← mimma I “and sim. anything, something”; mādiš ← mādiš I “greatly, very Bab., OA”; [t]ahših ← hašāhu I “to need, desire”
  • Note: See [RN117: 207–208]: “Tournay and Shaffer’s reading of the beginning of the line as [ni-še]-mi-im-[ma], ‘nous entendons’ ([RN580: 80, fn. 3]), does not convince on orthographic and contextual grounds. Although the idiom ana mādiš is not yet found before the Erra Epic (V 25), it is very tempting to read after mimma simply ammādiš (Foster).”
BabaOB1 i 14-15. [x (x)] x mi-im-ma [(x x)-a]m? ma-di-iš | [t]a-ah-ši-ih

16

  • N: ... [ ... ] ...
  • T: Let me … […] …
  • Note: See [RN117: 208]: “The first word was read lu-uš-šu-ú by Foster, who left it untranslated, and the whole line as lu-uš-ta-u₂ [aš-šum e-pi-i]š-tim, ‘je voudrais m’informer au sujet de l’entreprise’, by Tournay and Shaffer ([RN580: 80, fn. 4]). From šutawûm one would expect lu-uš-ta-wi, however, and the sign before tim is hardly iš. Other possibilities are lu-ús-si, ‘let me summon’, and lu-uš-ta-ú, ‘let me fly away’, but while the next word or words are undeciphered and the syntactic connection with šipram in l. 17 uncertain, it is best to speculate no further.”
BabaOB1 i 16. lu#-uš-x-u₂ [x (x)] x-tim

17

  • N: šipram | ša l[ā ib]aššû | ina mātim
  • T: a feat that does not (yet) exist in the land.’
  • L: šipram ← šipru I “pl. šiprū, Mari also šiprānu”; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; l[ā ← lā I “not, no”; ib]aššû ← bašû I “to be (at hand, available)”; ina ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; mātim ← mātu I “f. land, country”
  • Parallels: L I.4 OB "Harmal₁" 17b
BabaOB1 i 17. ši-ip-ra-am# ša l[a i-b]a-aš-šu-u₂ i-na KALAM

24

  • N: [arši | ibram || mā]likam | a[n]āk[u]
  • T: I [have acquired a friend, a] counsellor,
  • L: [arši ← rašû I “to acquire, get”; ibram ← ibru I “friend, colleague”; mā]likam ← māliku I “adviser, counsellor”; a[n]āk[u] ← anāku I “I”
  • Note: See [RN117: 208]: “These two lines of tablet are related to OB Schøyen obv. 2': Enkidu mālikam ša anāku ātammarūšu i[na šunātim]. However, l. 24 is squeezed in such a way that one suspects the presence of an additional word at the beginning of the line. I have restored accordingly (cf. OB Schøyen, obv. 1′).”

44

  • N: [līrub]ū-ma? | ana bīt (|) [šī]būti
  • T: ‘[…] go into the house [of the] elders.’
  • L: [līrub]ū-ma? ← erēbu I “to enter”; ana ← ana I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”; bīt ← bītu I “m.”; [šī]būti ← šību I “f. šībtu old (person)”
  • Note: See [RN117: 208]: “At the beginning Foster restores [iš-tu i-ru]-bu (though room is a little short), and Tournay and Shaffer [i-te-er]-bu, ‘ils entrèrent’ ([RN580: 81, fn. 10]). However, this is as likely direct speech as narrative, so [li-ru-b]u-ma, ‘let them go in’, also comes to mind. The reading bīt šībūti is Foster’s. CAD S, p. 10 (s.v. sābûtu), offers bīt [ši]-im-ti, citing OB Atram-ḫasīs I 249, but, as Foster notes, the sign bu is clear. Any reading sa-[x-b]u-ti is ruled out on orthographic grounds, sa not being a value used by this scribe (see above, fn. 7 of this chapter).”
BabaOB1 i 44. [x (x) x-b]u-ma a-na E₂# [ši?]-bu-ti

108

  • N: ana šūši | bērā || nummât | qištum
  • T: For sixty leagues the forest is a wilderness,
  • L: ana ← ana I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”; šūši ← šūši I “sixty elep šūši sixty(-gur) ship”; bērā ← bēru III “double hour, league”; nummât ← nawû II “to turn into desert”; qištum ← qištu I “pl. qišātu(m) forest, wood q. erēnim cedar forest”
  • Note: See [RN117: 209]: “For bērā see the study of the construction and writing of metrological units in the distributive by [powell1982adverbian]. As noted by [RN2652: 113], the sign before danna is not IGI-gunû (i.e., 10,000) but an abbreviated ligature of šu-ši. The SB text has 60-šu bēr and would hardly be guilty of a revision downwards. The penultimate word has been read in several different ways: Jastrow and Clay proposed nu-ma-at, which Langdon connected nu-ma-at with ‘Arabic nawa’ ([langdon1929notes: 346]). Thompson read bat-ba-at < battubattu, though this word is not found outside Assyria. Then Landsberger proposed til-ma-at, ‘ist umgeben’ (loc. cit.), which he derived from the root √lwʾ, supposing an exceptional metathesis tilmât < litwât. In support of this decipherment he cited RI-ma-at in SB II 293, which he read as tal-ma-at (‘Überlieferungsfehler für tilmât oder Plural von talwītu’). However, now that the SB word is securely deciphered as rimmat, after the parallels elsewhere in SB II (223 and 280), and now that Assyrian MS y₂ obv. 13’ supplies another word again (lamâssu), the reading til-ma-at has lost all foundation and looks very implausible on orthographic and lexical grounds (see already C. Wilcke, RLA IV, p. 533). The way out of the difficulty is to accept that the OB word is not related to its later counterparts and to assume that later editors, to whom nu-ma-at was obscure, replaced it and otherwise altered the line –in SB II by interpolating išemmēma— to produce a satisfactory meaning. Schott’s original comment that nu-ma-at must be a stative governed by qištum holds good ([schott1934zu: 108]), and the only possible verb in our present knowledge of Akkadian is nawûm. Though often translated as ‘to lie in ruins, to be laid waste’, the sense of this verb seems to be as much to do with a lack of human presence as to do with ruined buildings (cf. the cognate noun nawûm, which refers to the uninhabited regions beyond the arable land, the great tracts of largely empty country where sheep were pastured). The absence of human occupation is a conception which suits every occurrence and exactly fits the inaccessible and unvisited Cedar Forest (cf. von Soden, ‘liegt unberührt’: Reclam⁴ ⁵). Consequently I take the verb to mean ‘to be(come) a desolation, wilderness'. The stative of the II/1 adjective will be an elative of the simple stem. The fact that we have nummât rather than nuwwât is no objection in the light of the existence in good OB contexts of comparable attestations of the cognate noun (MSL XII, p. 158, OB Lu A 263: na-me-e; XIII, p. 229, Kagal I ii 62: na-mu-u₂, late OB). The three couplets that begin with this line are repeated as ll. 195-200.” Attia ([NABU2005-77]) suggested understanding the signs as NU ma-at, “c’est plus le Pays, c’est la Forêt.” See [RN2651: 10b]: “Recently Attia (2005) proposed NU ma-at, “c’est plus le Pays, c’est la Forêt.” The result is not far from the author’s translation, but epigraphically it is not possible to accept this suggestion. First, nowhere in the OB epic is lā written with NU. Secondly, the suggested double nominal phrase lā māt qištum, though theoretically not impossible, is not convincing. The typical way to construct nominal phrases in the epic is found in iii 110-112, and in iii 132. In addition, mātum is a neutral term for any land, not necessarily for a civilized one (which would probably be dadmii). Hence, lā māt is “ce n’est pas le pays,” and not with capital “c’est plus le Pays.” Further, the sentence begins with a prepositional phrase that logically leads to what was “for sixty leagues in each direction …,” not to what was not. And finally, the Cedar Forest is not found on the fringes of civilization, near the city of Uruk and Sumer in general, but miles away from the comrades’ home. Thus, even if mātum could designate “civilization,” the heroes have left the civilized world much earlier.”
  • Parallels: L I.4 OB "III" 195; L I.4 SB "II" 223; L I.4 SB "II" 293; L I.4 NA "y" a+13'
BabaOB1 iii 15'. a-na 1 šu+ši DANNA.TA.AM₃ nu-ma-at qi₂-iš-tum

  • T: who is there can venture inside it?

Neither dictionary accepts J. V. Kinnier Wilson’s bold contention that warādum can refer to upward motion as well as downward (in Garelli, Gilg., p. 106, fn. 1).” [RN2651: 10b]: “Jn fact, warādum, besides designating spatial descent, carries also the meaning of advancing, in any direction, with inimical intention.”

  • L: [huw]āwa ← Humbaba I; rigmašu ← rigmu I “pl. f. voice, cry, noise voice of deity, human”; abūbu ← abūbu I “flood, deluge Bab.”
  • Note: See [RN117: 209–210]: “110-12 // 197-8. This couplet is taken over unchanged into the late text (SB II 221-2 // 278-9 // 291-2). The second line also appears in OB Nippur 14 // rev. 3′, describing an Anzû-bird, and, with a minor alteration, in Assyrian MS y₂ obv. 12′. The wording is reminiscent of the description of Ḫuwawa in the Sumerian tale: ur.sag zu₂.zu₂.ni zu₂ ušumgal.la.kam | igi.ni igi pirig.ga₂.kam | giš.gaba.ni a.gi₆ du₇.du₇.dam | sag.ki.ni giš.gi bi₂.gu₇.a lu₂ nu.mu.da.te.ga₂.e.dam (Bilgames and Ḫuwawa A 99-102, ed. [RN195: 200]): “The warrior’s teeth are the teeth of a dragon, | his eye is the eye of a lion, | his breastbone is a surging flood-wave, | his forehead is (fire) that consumes a reed-bed: | no man is to go near him!” In ll. 110 // 197 the form rigmašu in place of the regular rigimšu is a rare example in OB Gilgameš of high literary style. For other examples of the pronominal suffixes attached to *pars/pirs/purs nouns in this way see [RN999: 214] (but note that zērāšu, given there as an OAkk example, is a regular accusative of a noun from a finally weak root in triptotic declension before the suffix). For such formations in the SB text see Ch. 9, the section on Language and style, sub (i).” [RN2651: 10b–11a] takes ri-ig-ma-šu as a dual.

What is restored before ibrī depends on how one construes what comes after. The reading adopted here goes back to Schott (Reclam²: “ich will ihren Berg ersteigen”). Though the verb elûm is very seldom construed with the object climbed in the accusative outside the fixed idiomatic usage of the same phrase, e.g. šadâšu īli, meaning a person disappeared-note the construction ēlû šamāʾī in l. 140 below and the repeated phrase nīlû šadâ in the late text (SB VIII 52, X 31 // 128 // 228). But there are other possibilities: (a) emend to lu-li a-<na> ša-di-ša, (b) interpret the signs as lūli aš-šadîša (so [ebeling1932review: 228]; [LS304: 213]; AHw, p. 206; CAD E, p. 118), which would be an example, unique in this text, of the apocopated preposition prefixed to the noun, or (c) abandon the possessive suffix and boldly posit a new adverb, šadîšam, ‘mountainwards’ (cf. GAG §67g). Scott’s reading and solutions (a) and (b), with their fem. possessive, preclude the restoration of masc. erēnum and favour [ša qištim]. Solution (c) would make an anticipatory genitive of this sort unlikely and the old staple [al-kam] would then recommend itself.”

Though others have thought differently–Tigay reads i-[din-šu {den-lil?]} ([RN809: 283]), Tournay and Shaffer read it-[ta-al-bi-iš] ([RN580: 85, fn. 40])–I assume that the OB line ends in the same way. With regard to the first word, von Soden noted ([LS304: 213]) that the value ḫá for HI.A is not found in Akkadian context but proposed the reading pu-ul-ḫá-tim nevertheless; the value has found its way into his syllabary ([AkkSyll: 47]). This strategy is unnecessary, however, for ‘broken’ fem. pl. nouns are an occasional feature of Akkadian (I owe this observation and the following references to W. G. Lambert): OB i-na um-me-a-tim (ummātim) um-šum ib-ba-aš-ši, ‘in summer there will be a heatwave’ (YOS X 22, 22); MB be-el ma-ti-a-ti (mātāti), ‘lord of the lands’ (BE I 41+46, 2; Kurigalzu); LB a-ba-aš-lam i-na gi-ninda₂-na-kum u₂-ma-an-di-da mi-in-di-a-tam (mindāti), ‘the surveyor measured the dimensions with a twelve-cubit rod’ (BE I 84 ii 25-7, cf. 38 mi-in-di-a-tim; Nbp). Note also, in this book, a ‘broken’ dual, bir-ki-a-šú for birkāšu in a LB manuscript (SB I 200, MS n).” For more examples of “broken” fem. pl., see [NABU2004-49] and [RN3043: 206 fn. 2].

  • N: gilgāmeš | itti huwāwa (|) dapīnim || taqumtam | ištu
  • T: (men will say) “Gilgameš joined battle with ferocious Ḫuwawa!”
  • L: gilgāmeš ← Gilgameš I; itti ← itti I “with”; huwāwa ← Humbaba I; dapīnim ← dapīnu I “overbearing, savage Bab., NA(lit.) epith. of god, king, lion etc.”; taqumtam ← tuqumtu I “battle Bab.(lit.)”; ištu ← šatû III “to knot together, weave Bab.”
  • Note: See [RN117: 211]: “I agree with W. G. Lambert that the first sign is not tu ([RN416: 271], from the unpublished copy of Shaffer) but to my eyes it is ta rather than iš. The spelling ta-qum-tam is meant for tuqumtam, as anticipated by [vonsoden1955boehl: 514], and newly confirmed by the Assyrian MS y₁ 5’, which has the logogram GIŠ.LA₂. A similar syllabic spelling is also known from an OB school textbook from Nippur ([RN1308: 4, 14′]: {ki-še-eš-bi|UR×UR|} = a-šar ta-qum-tim#); the existence of two examples of this form of the word implies lexical variation of the kind exhibited by the pair tarbuʾtum : turbuʾtum. The expression tuqumtam šatûm is a vividly figurative idiom, literally ‘to weave battle’, that likens the parry and thrust of man-to-man combat to the interlacing of warp and weft on the loom. It occurs in other texts: in an OB legend about Narām-Sîn ([temp_id_8614570978802014: 191, i 1]; also [RN262: 278]): qa₂-ab-lam iš-ta-tu i-na mu-uh-hi-ša#, ‘he joined battle against her (or it)’; in Bullussa-rabi’s hymn to Gula ([RN775: 122, 111]): šá-tu-ú a-na-an-tum, ‘(Ninurta), who joins combat’; and in a late hymn to Ninurta ([RN358: 21, 2a]): [i]-na qe₂-reb te-še-e a-šar ša₂-ta-at a-nun-tu, ‘in the midst of havoc, where combat is joined'. The image is elaborated in a bilingual litany which celebrates the goddess Inanna’s role in combat ([RN1719: 200], Uruammairrabi XXI 72): me₃.a gu mu.dun.dun // ina ta-ha-zi qe₂-e a-šat-tu₄, “in battle I interweave the threads”.”

  • Note: See [RN117: 212]: “A ṣiprum is typically a tapering projection like a horn or a comet’s tail (see CAD Ṣ, s.v.). Here the word occurs in a line that falls between those describing the daggers’ blades and pommels and are qualified as being ‘of the blades’ sides’. The reference can only be to a projecting crossguard that keep the user’s hand from slipping on to the blade (so already Labat: ‘crête de leur garde’). Good examples of blades furnished with such projections are the famous gold daggers from the royal cemetery at Ur. The curved guard projects out from the blade on either side in the manner of two horns or crests (photographs: Woolley, UE II, pls. 155, 157).”

  • Note: See [RN117: 214]: “In the absence of a preposition before Gilgameš, u₂-GA-ra-bu is hardly qurrubum, ‘to approach’ ([RN272]). Despite the contrasting spelling of i-ka-ra-bu-šu in l. 247 the verb of the present line must also be a form of karābu. The spelling represents a survival of third-millennium practice. The verb takes the present tense because, as a verbum dicendi, it introduces speech.”
BabaOB1 vi 16'. [GURUŠ?-M]EŠ u₂-ka₃-ra-bu {d}GIŠ

246

  • N: [ ... ] ... | tuttēr | ana libbi (|) āli
  • T: ‘[…] you (shall?) have sent back inside the city.’
  • L: tuttēr ← târu I “to turn, return”; ana ← ana I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”; libbi ← libbu I “inner body”; āli ← ālu I “m., Am. occas. f.”
  • Note: See [RN117: 214]: “Von Soden took the verb as II/2 preterite, restored [ina m]a-ti, and translated ‘Wann würdest du zurückgebracht in die Stadt?’, but with the comment ‘es ist nicht klar, … was damit gemeint wird’ ([LS304: 214]; see similarly Reclam⁴⁻⁵ but note Reclam²: ‘bring zurück zur Stadt!’). Others have translated similarly (Dalley, Hecker), or as if the verb was a simple I/1 present, either as a question (Heidel, Labat, Bottéro, and, restoring [im-m]a-ti, [RN580: 95, fn. 98]), a wish (Speiser) or a prediction (Pettinato). The verb is unsuited to a question relating to Gilgameš’s anticipated return--unless it is future perfect, i.e. II/1 transitive and notably lacks the ventive ending that would be expected if it referred to the hero’s homecoming. Apart from the problems raised by tuttēr, the first word is also open to doubt: Clay’s copy did not suggest that the broken sign could be ma and to my eyes it is more like ne. Rather than an interrogative, the broken word might be the object of transitive tuttēr.”
BabaOB1 vi 17'. [x] x-ti tu-ut-te-er a-na ŠA₃ URU{ki}

247-248

  • N: [šīb]ūtum | ikarrabūšu | [an]a harrānim | imallikū | gilgāmeš
  • T: [The] elders blessed Gilgameš, giving him advice for the journey:
  • L: [šīb]ūtum ← šību I “f. šībtu old (person)”; ikarrabūšu ← karābu II “to pray, bless, greet”; [an]a ← ana I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”; harrānim ← harrānu I “f., later also m. way, road”; imallikū ← malāku II “to discuss”; gilgāmeš ← Gilgameš I
  • Note: See [RN602: 408]: “ikarrabū übersetzt George zu Recht mit „blessed“, denn das Präsens ist durch die folgende direkte Rede bedingt. Dies gilt dann aber auch für imallikū in derselben Zeile, das somit keinen Umstandssatz der Gleichzeitigkeit darstellt: „Die Ältesten segneten Gilgames und gaben ihm für die Reise den Rat: …“”
BabaOB1 vi 18'-19'. [ši-b]u-tum i-ka-ra#-bu-šu | [a-n]a KASKAL i-ma-li-ku {d}GIŠ

  • T: ‘[Do not] rely, O Gilgameš, on your strength (alone)!

  • Parallels: cf. L I.4 SB "III" 3; cf. L I.4 SB "III" 217; cf. L I.4 OB "III" 256
BabaOB1 vi 21'. [i-n]a-ka lu šu-wu-ra-ma u₂-ṣur ra-ma-an-ka

  • T: [Let] Enkidu go before you,

  • Parallels: L I.4 SB "III" 6; L I.4 SB "III" 77; L I.4 SB "III" 220
BabaOB1 vi 22'. [li-i]l-lik {d}+en-ki-du₁₀ i-na pa-ni-ka

  • Note: See [RN117: 214]: “The tablet has a-me-er, as already copied by Clay and Shaffer (unpublished). The reading a-we-ir put forward by Jastrow and Clay ([YOSR_3_IV: 94]) is presumably a misprint or uncorrected error, unfortunately repeated by [RN2980], and revived by [edzard1994namir: 2].”
  • Parallels: cf. L I.4 SB "III" 8; cf. L I.4 SB "III" 222

  • N: [īd]e | ša qišti | nērebētim
  • T: [He knows] the ways into the forest,

254

  • N: [ša h]uwāwa | kalīšunu | šibqīšu
  • T: all the tricks of Huwawa.
  • L: [ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; h]uwāwa ← Humbaba I; kalīšunu ← kalû II “all, totality”; šibqīšu ← šibqū I “pl. tant. scheme, plan”
  • Note: See [RN117: 214]: “The reading šibqīšu goes back to [vonsoden1955boehl: 514], though the penultimate sign turns out to be qi₄, rather than qì (as also in pa-ás-na-qi₄, l. 156).”

255

  • N: [āl]ik | mahra || tappâm | ušallim
  • T: “The one who went in front kept his comrade safe;
  • L: [āl]ik ← alāku I “to go”; mahra ← mahra I “in front”; tappâm ← tappû I “companion, partner friend”; ušallim ← šalāmu II “to be(come) healthy, intact”
  • Note: See [RN117: 214–215]: “255–6. The couplet is remarkable for the tense of its verbs. In l. 256 there is hardly room to restore i-[na-ṣa-ar] and ušallim in l. 255 is certainly preterite. Some have ignored the tense, while others have seen an allusion to some otherwise unknown episode in which Enkidu saved a companion earlier in his career. The key, however, is the phenomenon recently discussed by [RN2725]. Mayer observed that in texts such as the Šamaš Hymn and Marduk Prayer No. 2 the preterite tense is found alongside the present and stative in verbs that refer to the typical: ‘Bei Aussagen über typische Situationen, Geschehnisse, Handlungen und Verhaltensweisen finden wir hier nämlich nebeneinander den Stativ, das Präsens-und das Präteritum, letzeres manchmal sogar in Parallelismus mit einem Präsens’ (p. 392). The parallelism he notes is exactly that occurring between ušezzeb and iṣṣur in the late version of this couplet (SB III 4-5: ālik maḫri tappâ ušezzeb / ša ṭūdu īdû ibiršu iṣṣur, cf. SB III 218-19). Mayer expected to find the ‘gnomic preterite’ in Akkadian proverbs and everyday expressions but noted just one example. I am inclined to think that this couplet contains two more (Kovacs took the same view of the late equivalent of the couplet). Other apparently proverbial sayings in SB Gilgameš using the ‘gnomic preterite’ are to be found in SB VII 75-6: ana balṭi […] īzibū nasāsa / [mī]tu(?) ana balṭi nissata īzib; VII 86-7: [ša i]qbû ul itūr ul i[pšiṭ] / … iddû ul itūr ul ipšiṭ X 318 var.: lullâ mītu ul ikruba (karābi) ina māti.” See also [RN602: 408]: “Das gnomische Präteritum wurde auch in Zahl und Zeit S. 145-147 § 31 behandelt; dort sind auch weitere Belege aus dem Akkadischen genannt.”
  • Parallels: L I.4 SB "III" 4; L I.4 SB "III" 218
BabaOB1 vi 26'. [a-li]k mah-ra tap-pa-a u₂-ša-lim

  • N: [ša ī]nāšu | šuwwurā || pagaršu | iṣṣ[ur?]
  • T: the one whose eyes were peeled [protected] himself!”
  • L: [ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; ī]nāšu ← īnu I “f. eye”; šuwwurā ← nawāru I “to be(come) bright, shine”; pagaršu ← pagru I “pl. pagrū, jB also f., NB also pagrānu body”; iṣṣ[ur?] ← naṣāru I “to guard, protect”
  • Parallels: L I.4 SB "III" 5; L I.4 SB "III" 219; cf. L I.4 SB "III" 135; cf. L I.4 OB "III" 250
BabaOB1 vi 27'. [ša i]-na-šu šu-wu-ra pa#-gar₃#-šu# i#-ṣ[u₂-ur?]

  • N: [liša]kšidka | ernittaka | šamš[u]
  • T: May Šamaš allow you to achieve your ambition,
  • L: [liša]kšidka ← kašādu I “to reach, arrive”; ernittaka ← ernittu I “triumph, battle objective Bab.(lit.), NB e. kašādu to achieve…”; šamš[u] ← šamšu I “OB occas. f. sun”
  • Parallels: L I.4 OB "III" 286
BabaOB1 vi 28'. [li-ša-a]k-ši!#(TI)-id#-ka# er-ni-ta#-ka {d}UTU-š[u]

  • T: may your eyes show (you) what you have talked of!

BabaOB1 vi 29'. na#-aq-bi-a-at pi-ka li-kal-li-ma i-na-k[a]

259

  • N: liptēkum | padānam | pehītam
  • T: May he open for you the paths that are shut,
  • L: liptēkum ← petû II “to open”; padānam ← padānu I “f. & m. way, path OAkk, Bab.”; pehītam ← pehû I “sealed, closed”
BabaOB1 vi 30'. li-ip-te-kum pa-da-nam pe-hi-tam

260

  • N: harrānam | lištassiq | ana kibsīka
  • T: may he ready the road for your footsteps!
  • L: harrānam ← harrānu I “f., later also m. way, road”; lištassiq ← nasāqu I “to choose, select”; ana ← ana I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”; kibsīka ← kibsu I “pl. m. & f. track, footprint”
  • Parallels: cf. L I.4 SB "III" 79
BabaOB1 vi 31'. KASKAL li-iš-ta-si₂-iq a-na ki-ib-si₂-ka

  • N: šadia(m) | lištassiq | ana šēpīka
  • T: May he ready the mountain for your feet,
  • L: šadia(m) ← šadû I “st. constr. šad(i)”; lištassiq ← nasāqu I “to choose, select”; ana ← ana I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”; šēpīka ← šēpu I “f., often du.”
  • Note: See [RN117: 215]: “The spelling ša-di-a attests to a ‘hypercorrect’ uncontracted form of šadûm a false archaism that also occurs in OB Schøyen₂ 5. The word for ‘mountain’ (originally šadwum?) is given in OAkk and some OB texts as šaduʾum; the homophonous word šadûm, ‘east wind’, however, in uncontracted form appears as šadiʾum in Akkadian of the third millennium ([RN1286: 264-5]) and as a loanword in OB Sumerian ([RN1664ax: 71, 4, 9]: {imsa₁₂.ti.um}).”
  • Parallels: cf. L I.4 SB "III" 79
BabaOB1 vi 32'. ša-di-a li-iš-ta-si₂-iq a-na GIR₃-ka

  • N: mušītka | awāt (|) tahaddû | liblakku
  • T: may each night bring you a thing you will be glad of!
  • L: mušītka ← mūšu I “night”; awāt ← awātu I “word”; tahaddû ← hadû III “to be joyful, rejoice”; liblakku ← wabālu I “(cf. also babālu) to carry, bring”
  • Note: See [RN117: 215]: “263–4. These lines present an instance–exceptional for the Pennsylvania and Yale tablets–of the boundary between two poetic lines falling in the middle of a line of tablet. With regard to lizziz-ka, in the idiom ‘to aid’ izuzzum is normally construed with the dative suffix, not the accusative (as pointed out by Hecker, TUAT II/4, p. 658).” See also [RN602: 408]: “mušītka ist nicht „each night“, sondern einfach „Nacht“. Der angebliche semantische Unterschied zwischen mūšum und mušītum existiert m. E. nicht, mušītum ist lediglich eine Rückbildung aus dem bisweilen femininen Plural des Wortes mūšum; vgl. Rez., ZA 95 (2005) 148. Vgl. das zu OB Schøyen₂ 54 Gesagte.” But cf. [RN2651: 11b]: “‘May each night bring you a thing you will be glad of!’' For the use of mušītum as nomen unitatis in OB literature, see [RN547: 71–73].”

  • T: May Lugalbanda assist you in your victory;
  • L: lugalbanda ← Lugalbanda I; lizzizka ← izuzzu I “to stand”; ina ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; ernittīka ← ernittu I “triumph, battle objective Bab.(lit.), NB e. kašādu to achieve…”
BabaOB1 vi 34'b-35'. {d}lugal-ban₃-da li-iz-zi-iz-ka | i-na er-ni-ti-ka

  • N: kīma ṣehrim | ernittaka | kušda(m)
  • T: attain your desire like a little child!
  • L: kīma ← kīma I “like”; ṣehrim ← ṣehru I “small”; ernittaka ← ernittu I “triumph, battle objective Bab.(lit.), NB e. kašādu to achieve…”; kušda(m) ← kašādu I “to reach, arrive”
  • Note: See [RN117: 215]: “The opinion of Oppenheim, that kīma ṣeḫrim is simply a way of saying ‘quickly’ ([RN729: 33, fn. 2]; cf. [RN2165: 269, fn. 103]), must be modified in the light of the evidence of the OB love incantations from Isin, which reveal that ernittam kīma ṣeḫrim kašādum is a stock image: a-di ki-ma ṣe₂-eh-ri-im e-le-eq-qu₂-u₂ er-ni-[it-ti], ‘until, like a child, I obtain my own way’ ([wilcke1985liebesbeschwoerungen: 204, 111]); cf. also am-mi-ni ki-ma ṣe-eh-ri-im la-hi-im er-ni-it-ta-ka le-em-ne₂-et, ‘why, like a tiny child, is your (insistence on getting) what you want so annoying?’ (ibid., p. 200, 54). In Wilcke’s words, ‘es ist vielmehr das Bild des hartnäckig entgegen jeder Vernunft auf der Erfüllung seiner Wünsche bestehenden Kindes gemeint’ (ibid., p. 207).” See also [RN602: 408]: “Für den Vergleich kīma ṣeḫri s. Bildersprache S. 62 Nr. 16; danach ist eine Wurzel des Vergleichs die Deutung des in Z. 263 genannten Namens Lugalbanda als „kleiner König“.”
BabaOB1 vi 36'. ki-ma ṣe-eh-ri er-ni-ta-ka ku-uš-da

266

  • N: ina nārim | ša huwāwa | ša tuṣammaru
  • T: In Huwawa’s river, for which you are aiming,
  • L: ina ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; nārim ← nāru I “f., NA m. river, watercourse, canal”; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; huwāwa ← Humbaba I; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; tuṣammaru ← ṣamāru I “to wish, strive (for)”
  • Note: See [RN117: 215]: “266–7. The ‘river of Ḫuwawa’ is otherwise unknown and does not quite ring true as the object of Gilgameš’s strivings: his stated ambitions are to defeat Ḫuwawa by force of arms and to fell the cedars under his protection. One thus has some sympathy for those who prefer nârum, ‘to slay’, to nārum, ‘river’, but Speiser’s rendering, ‘after the slaying of Ḫuwawa’, mistranslates ina nârim, which as an infinitive construction would mean ‘while slaying, by slaying'. As the text stands this would be a curious way of inciting Gilgameš to stand awash in Ḫuwawa’s blood and accordingly I have stayed with ‘river'. But it may be that we are misled by a defective text, for l. 267 misi šēpīka is unusually short for a poetic line.” Note, in addition, the absence of trochaic ending in l. 266.

BabaOB1 vi 40'. lu ka-a-a-nu A SIKIL i-na na-di-ka

  • N: [k]aṣûtim | mê | ana šamši | tanaqqi
  • T: You must pour cool water (in libation) to Šamaš,
  • L: [k]aṣûtim ← kaṣû I “f. kaṣītu cold Bab., NA of water”; mê ← mû I “pl. tant. water mê kabrūtim mass of water”; ana ← ana I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”; šamši ← šamšu I “OB occas. f. sun”; tanaqqi ← naqû I “to pour (a libation), sacrifice”

  • N: [ilk]a | tahassas | lugalbanda
  • T: you must remember your [god,] Lugalbanda.’

  • Note: See [RN117: 215]: “For Lugalbanda as the personal god (ilum) of Gilgameš in the Akkadian epic, see explicitly OB Nippur 8, OB Harmal 15-16 and SB VI 165.”
BabaOB1 vi 42'. [il-k]a ta-ha-sa₃-as {d}lugal-ban₃-da

272

  • N: [enkīd]u | pīšu | īpušam | issaqqar | ana gilgāmeš
  • T: Enkidu opened his mouth, saying to Gilgameš:
  • L: [enkīd]u ← Enkidu I; pīšu ← pû I “(also OB)”; īpušam ← epēšu II “to do”; issaqqar ← zakāru I “to speak, say”; ana ← ana I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”; gilgāmeš ← Gilgameš I
BabaOB1 vi 43'. [{d}+en-ki-d]u₁₀ pi-šu i#-pu-ša-am is-sa₃-qar a-na {d}GIŠ

273

  • N: [ ( ... ) aš]ar | taštaknu | epuš | alākam
  • T: ‘Where you are minded begin the journey,
  • L: aš]ar ← ašru III “pl. m. & f., place, site”; taštaknu ← šakānu I “to put, place, lay down”; epuš ← epēšu II “to do”; alākam ← alāku I “to go”
  • Note: See [RN117: 215]: “Von Soden read [ki]-ma ta-aš-tan-nu < šanānum I/2, ‘so, wie du gekämpfst hat’ ([LS304: 215]; cf. Speiser: ‘[Since] contend thou wilt’), and this decipherment has found its way into his syllabary as a parade example of OB use of the value tan ([AkkSyll: 33]; also AHw, p. 1162; CAD Š/1, p. 369). However, such a reading is very doubtful. First, the traces do not allow [ki]-ma. Second, the third sign of the verb is not certainly tan. There is no example of the syllabic value tan elsewhere in the Pennsylvania and Yale tablets (the only time the syllable is written it is spelled ta-an: OB II 204), but when the KAL sign is used, on occasion for eṭlum (guruš: II 147, 193, III 283), it does not match the sign in question here, which has too many vertical wedges to be read so. Instead it compares favourably with the certain ták in l. 188. But there remains a problem of meaning: given that taštaknu should be transitive, whether I/1 or I/2, what is its object? With some hesitation I assume that the phrase is an abbreviation of the idiom ašar pānīka taštaknu.” See also the restoration [iš-t]u proposed by [RN2651: 11b]: “[sin]ce you have already been equipped, begin the journey!”

275

  • N: [ina qi]šti | īdeam | šupassu
